Root-Cause Hypothesis: RTP and manual scan may use different definition versions, archive handling, exclusions, or verdict normalization. The screenshots do not establish which path is responsible.

Example Scenario to Validate: In an isolated VM, scan the same inert EICAR test file after a definition update: first on write via RTP, then on demand from the identical path and hash.

Expected vs. Reported Behavior: Expected: both scan paths use the same definition generation and return a consistent detection/quarantine result. Reported: a sample was called clean in a manual scan while RTP reportedly detected it; reproduce before assigning root cause.

text: Root-Cause Hypothesis: Protected-resource ACLs, service access controls, or kernel enforcement may be absent or insufficient for the tested account and installation state. Example Scenario to Validate: On a disposable, authorized test VM, attempt a rename and write to a signed product binary as a standard user and as an elevated administrator; capture the exact access result and product logs. Expected vs. Reported Behavior: Expected: unauthorized mutation is denied and audited while supported update/repair flows remain functional. Reported: AV files could reportedly be renamed or modified; the privilege level and exact file are not documented.

text: Root-Cause Hypothesis: Category taxonomy, wildcard/apex matching, allow/deny precedence, or policy cache refresh may be inconsistent across browser, DNS, and encrypted traffic paths. Example Scenario to Validate: In a controlled test profile, classify a documented chat-domain test set, add one domain to the allowlist, apply the policy without reboot, and test apex plus subdomain variants over HTTPS. Expected vs. Reported Behavior: Expected: the chat category and explicit allowlist produce deterministic, documented precedence across supported traffic paths. Reported: WhatsApp categorization/allowlisting failed and a restricted chat site remained accessible.
author: Admin

text: Root-Cause Hypothesis: Category feed coverage, refresh cadence, domain normalization, and keyword-rule scope may vary; the estimate is user-reported rather than a measured benchmark. Example Scenario to Validate: Build a dated, legally approved QA corpus with expected categories; test parent domains, subdomains, redirects, and a fresh taxonomy sync, recording false positives and false negatives. Expected vs. Reported Behavior: Expected: documented category coverage is versioned and repeatable, with block/allow outcomes matching the test corpus. Reported: only 20–40% coverage on a tested category, while explicit blacklist tests were positive.
author: Admin

text: Root-Cause Hypothesis: Selection state may be lost in bulk restore, quarantine metadata may not sync to exclusions, or UI/service calls may fail without isolated error handling. These are separate repro candidates. Example Scenario to Validate: Quarantine two harmless test files, restore only one, verify the other stays quarantined, then restart the UI and recheck exceptions. Separately exercise add-folder and delete flows with permission denial and interrupted service responses. Expected vs. Reported Behavior: Expected: only the selected item is restored, exception state persists, and failures surface without a crash. Reported: bulk restore, missing exception, add-folder crash, delete failure, and assessment mismatch require independent confirmation.

text:
Title: Desynchronization Between Real-Time and Manual Scan Detection

Severity: Critical
Priority: High
Component: Antivirus Engine / Scan Coordinator

Summary:
SiyanoAV exhibits conflicting detection results for the same malware sample depending on the scan method used. Real-time protection successfully identifies the threat, but the manual scan engine completely misses it. This strongly indicates that the two engines are operating with disparate definitions, heuristics, or database access.

Steps to Reproduce:

Verify that SiyanoAV Real-Time Protection is Active.

Navigate to a folder containing a known malware sample (e.g., hacktool.keylogger/msil).

Observe that Real-Time Protection blocks/quarantines the file (Confirm using visual evidence, e.g., image_0.png).

Disable Real-Time Protection.

Restore the infected file (if necessary/possible for testing).

Initiate a manual 'Virus Scanning' or 'Quick Scan' on that specific file or its parent folder.

Observe the final scan results.

Expected Result:
The manual scan should detect the exact same threat that the real-time protection identified.

Actual Result:
The manual scan completes successfully but reports "Threats Detected: 0" (Confirm using visual evidence, e.g., image_1.png). The infected file remains undetection.

Evidence:

Attached: image_2.png (Visual Report overlaying conflicting results and demonstrating engine desynchronization).

Proposed Solution:
The development team must enforce synchronization across all scanning modules. The software should utilize a centralized intelligence coordinator that ensures real-time and manual/on-demand scanning engines access the identical, most up-to-date virus definition database and utilize the same heuristic rules.
author: Sanjay

text:
Subject: CRITICAL SECURITY BREACH: Complete Lack of AV Self-Protection (Anti-Tamper)

Priority: Critical
Component: Antivirus Core / System Driver

Summary:
During a routine security audit, a fundamental architectural flaw was identified: SiyanoAV provides zero self-protection. The application's UI lacks a mechanism to enable/disable self-protection, and consequently, critical system files, registry keys, and running processes are completely vulnerable to tamper. Targeted malware can disable SiyanoAV by simply renaming its main executable, modifying core DLLs, or deleting its service, effectively crippling the protection suite before it can neutralize the threat.

Vulnerability Description:
Self-Protection is an industry-standard security measure for antivirus software. It prevents malware (or malicious users) from:

Terminating Running Processes: Stopping SiyanoAV Total Security.exe, services, or driver threads.

File Tampering: Deleting or renaming core components in C:\Program Files (x86)\Siyano Labs Pvt. Ltd\.

Registry Tampering: Deleting or modifying auto-start registry keys (HKLM or HKCU) that ensure the AV loads on boot.

Evidence:

Missing UI Mechanism: The current 'General Settings' panel (image_3.png) contains no toggle or configuration for 'Self-Protection' or 'Anti-Tamper'.

Vulnerability Mapping: The attached image (image_5.png) visually maps how the missing UI corresponds to immediate system vulnerabilities. It illustrates how an attacker can simulate renaming core files (like SiyanoAV Total Security.exe or BouncyCastle.Crypto.dll) to defeat the software's ability to protect itself.

Steps to Reproduce (Simulation):

Verify that SiyanoAV is fully updated and 'Realtime' protection is Active.

Open Windows Explorer and navigate to C:\Program Files (x86)\Siyano Labs Pvt. Ltd\SiyanoAV Total Security.

Attempt to rename a non-essential file like FontAwesome.WPF.dll to FontAwesome.WPF.dll.old. (Simulation successful, as shown in image_3.png/image_4.png).

(CRITICAL STEP) Attempt to rename a critical component, like SiyanoAV Total Security.exe.

Observation: SiyanoAV does not prevent this action.

Consequence: The main AV interface will fail to launch, or the real-time scanning engine will crash, leaving the system undefended.

Suggested Solution:

Immediate UI Update: Add a 'Self-Protection' (or 'Anti-Tamper') toggle to the 'Security' > 'General Settings' dashboard (image_3.png). This should be ON by default and require Administrative privileges (UAC) to modify.

Core Driver Implementation: Implement kernel-mode hook-based protection (or utilizes modern ELAM - Early Launch Anti-Malware) to intercept and block system calls (e.g., NtTerminateProcess, NtOpenProcess, CreateFile) directed at protected SiyanoAV resources (Processes, Services, Registry Keys, and the installation folder).
author: Sanjay

text:
SiyanoAV Firewall UI Rules Are Non-Functional and Fail to Filter Application Traffic

Severity: Critical

Priority: High

Component: Network / Firewall Module & WFP Driver

Summary
SiyanoAV Firewall fails to enforce user-configured firewall rules. Setting an application rule to "Block" (e.g., blocking Brave browser) does not drop or intercept network packets. The target application retains full internet connectivity. Comparative testing with native Windows Defender Firewall confirms that standard OS firewall blocking functions correctly, proving SiyanoAV's engine is disconnected from active filtering.

Steps to Reproduce
Open SiyanoAV Total Security and navigate to Security > Firewall > Rules.

Add or configure a rule to Block network access for a specific browser/application (e.g., Brave Browser).

Ensure the rule is toggled Active in the SiyanoAV dashboard.

Launch the target application (Brave Browser) and attempt to navigate to any external web address (e.g., [https://rentthelook.in](https://rentthelook.in)).

Observation: The webpage loads successfully without network restriction.

Comparative Test (Windows Defender Firewall)
Open wf.msc (Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security).

Create an Outbound Rule -> Program -> Select Executable -> Choose Block the connection.

Launch the target executable.

Observation: Traffic is dropped immediately, confirming Windows Filtering Platform (WFP) is working as expected.

Expected Result
SiyanoAV Firewall should intercept network traffic for configured applications and block inbound/outbound packets when a "Block" rule is set.

Actual Result
SiyanoAV Firewall rules have no effect on network traffic. Applications bypass SiyanoAV rules completely.

Root Cause Hypothesis
Driver Unbound: SiyanoAV network driver (WFP callout driver / NDIS filter) is either not installed, disabled, or failing to bind to active network adapters.

UI-to-Engine Disconnect: Front-end UI rule changes are saved locally (e.g., XML/JSON config) but are never passed down to the underlying kernel driver/service.
author: Sanjay

text:
Parental Control: WhatsApp Misclassified as Social Network & Whitelist Override Fails

Severity: High

Priority: High

Component: Parental Control / Web Categorization & Filtering Engine

Summary
The Parental Control module misclassifies WhatsApp under "Social networks" instead of "Games and chats". Additionally, explicitly adding web.whatsapp.com to the Whitelist fails to grant access when "Social networks" blocking is enabled, causing WhatsApp connections to fail continuously.

Steps to Reproduce
Launch SiyanoAV Total Security and navigate to Privacy > Parental Control Settings > Websites access by category.

Enable access restriction for "Social networks" (keep "Games and chats" disabled).

Open WhatsApp Web (web.whatsapp.com) or WhatsApp Desktop.

Observation 1: WhatsApp gets blocked immediately due to being categorized under Social Networks.

Navigate to White and Black lists of sites tab.

Add web.whatsapp.com as Allowed to the Whitelist.

Retry connecting on WhatsApp Web / Desktop.

Observation 2: The connection attempt still fails, returning "An unexpected error occurred".

Expected Result
WhatsApp should be classified under the "Games and chats" category.

Whitelisted domains (web.whatsapp.com) should bypass all category-based restrictions unconditionally.

Actual Result
Blocking "Social networks" restricts WhatsApp usage.

Adding web.whatsapp.com to the Whitelist has no effect, and access remains blocked.

Root Cause Hypothesis
Categorization DB: The cloud/local site-rating database maps whatsapp.com and web.whatsapp.com under Category: Social Media instead of Category: Instant Messaging / Chat.

Filter Rule Pipeline: The filtering driver prioritizes Category Deny rules over explicit Whitelist Accept rules. Whitelist checking must occur at step 0 in the lookup pipeline before category classification is queried.
author: Sanjay
